correctness.rationale: The degree-three residual gives a quadratic inverse polynomial with positive leading coefficient a_2. Multiplying A² gives the degree-sum edge test a_2 w_ij(μ+3Λ/2−d_i−d_j) on trees, one positive two-step product at distance two and zero at distances at least three. The Chebyshev residual has modulus less than one on the positive spectrum, so the inverse polynomial is positive definite and all diagonal entries are positive. Around an arbitrary edge, its incident double star has s+2=d_i+d_j vertices in the unweighted tree and its padded Laplacian is dominated in positive-semidefinite order by the full one. A quotient on the two hubs and two constant leaf blocks yields the cubic; absent leaf blocks introduce only redundant unit roots. At z=2(s+2)/3 its value is maximized by balancing the leaf counts because the coefficient multiplying kℓ is z>0. The ten exact balanced values for s=0,…,9 are negative, so the largest root exceeds z. This proves the all-shift assertion through order eleven. Factoring the symmetric cubic gives the claimed largest eigenvalue and cutoff, positive exactly for m≥5; the outside edge degree sum is smaller than 3Λ/2, and the explicit m=5, μ=1/4 bridge radical is strictly negative. Thus the failure at twelve is existential and sharp, not a claim that all twelve-vertex trees fail.
residual_risks: The order cut-off applies to unweighted connected trees and the completed exact-endpoint degree-three residual; it does not apply to intermediate stages or claim a weighted order cut-off. Numerical tree enumeration is not needed for the universal claim.
